prompt: Explain how compound interest works.
answer:
Compound interest is a financial concept that refers to the process of earning interest on not just the original amount deposited or invested, but also on the interest that is earned each period. 

Here is an example to illustrate how compound interest works. Let's say you deposit $1,000 into a savings account with an annual interest rate of 5%. With simple interest, at the end of the first year, you would earn $50 in interest, giving you a total balance of $1,050. In the second year, you would again earn 5% interest on the original $1,000 deposit, giving you another $50 in interest and a balance of $1,100.

But with compound interest, you would earn $50 in interest in the first year, just like with simple interest. However, in the second year, you would earn 5% interest not just on the original $1,000, but on the new balance of $1,050. This means that in the second year, you would earn $52.50 in interest, bringing your total balance to $1,102.50.

As you can see, with compound interest, you earn additional interest on the interest that you have already earned. This means that your balance grows at an accelerating rate over time.

Compound interest can work in your favor when it comes to saving and investing your money, as it allows your money to grow more quickly over time. However, it can work against you when it comes to borrowing money, as you will end up paying more in interest over the life of the loan.

Due to this tilt, the orientation of Earth with respect to the Sun changes over the course of a year, and different areas of Earth receive different amount of solar radiation (also called insolation) at any given point of time.
